title: FIFTEEN YEARS: My Wife Left Seven Boxes After I Spent a Week in Rome With My Mistress—What I Discovered Destroyed My Billion-Dollar Empire
excerpt: My name is Gabriel Laurent. I’m forty-three years old, and according to every financial magazine that has ever written about me, I’m worth approximately $5.9 billion.
author: admin

blocks.text: My name is Gabriel Laurent. I’m forty-three years old, and according to every financial magazine that has ever written about me, I’m worth approximately $5.9 billion.
I own luxury hotels in twelve countries, a private aviation company, commercial properties across Europe, and a technology investment firm headquartered in New York.
I’ve appeared on magazine covers. I’ve shaken hands with presidents. I’ve bought buildings simply because I liked the view from the penthouse.
For fifteen years, I had one woman beside me.
She was thirty-nine, beautiful in a quiet way, intelligent, compassionate, and far more patient than I deserved.
But somewhere along the way, I began confusing her patience with weakness.
And most importantly, I thought my money made me untouchable.
I was standing in my office when Isabelle called.
“Isabelle, we discussed this. The investors are expecting me.”
“I need to tell you something important.”
I looked at the photograph on my desk. It showed Isabelle and me on our wedding day, fifteen years earlier.
She was smiling so brightly that I almost didn’t recognize the woman in the picture.
My private jet was scheduled to depart in two hours.
“Listen, sweetheart. I’ll be back next Monday. We’ll talk then. I promise.”
I didn’t know that would be the last conversation we would have as husband and wife.
I was taking Victoria, my thirty-one-year-old mistress.
Victoria was a former model I’d met at a charity gala six months earlier. She was glamorous, ambitious, and fascinated by my wealth.
She liked expensive restaurants, designer handbags, and photographs of herself in front of beautiful places.
Unlike Isabelle, Victoria never asked me to slow down.
She never asked why I came home at midnight.
For seven days, we lived like royalty in Rome.

We stayed in a private penthouse overlooking the city. We ate at restaurants where reservations were almost impossible to obtain. We visited museums after closing hours and drank champagne on a terrace overlooking ancient rooftops.
Victoria posted photographs of our trip, carefully avoiding my face.
“You’re sure your wife won’t find out?” she asked one evening.
“Isabelle doesn’t concern herself with my business.”
“Victoria, my wife knows how this world works. She’s comfortable. She has everything she could possibly want.”
There were four missed calls from Isabelle.
Those words would haunt me for the rest of my life.
On Sunday evening, I received another message.
By Monday afternoon, I was back in Paris.
Victoria wanted me to stay with her for another night, but I told her I had to return home.
Despite everything, I expected her to greet me at the door.
I’d buy her something expensive. A necklace, perhaps. Maybe a trip to the Maldives.
Or at least, I’d convinced myself it had.
My driver brought me to our mansion shortly after six.
And Isabelle’s car wasn’t in the driveway.
I placed my suitcase near the staircase and headed upstairs.
When I opened our bedroom door, I stopped breathing.
Every dress, every handbag, every pair of shoes was gone.
The jewelry boxes she kept on the dressing table had disappeared.
Even the little photograph of us beside the mirror was missing.
The only things remaining were seven large wooden boxes arranged in a perfect row on the floor.
Each box had a number painted on its lid.
Its screen displayed a single video file.
I picked up the tablet and pressed play.
She was sitting in the living room, wearing a simple blue sweater.
“Gabriel,” she began softly. “If you’re watching this, you’ve finally come home.”
“I begged you to stay with me for one week. You chose Rome instead.”
“I know about Victoria. I know about the hotel, the private dinners, and the photographs you thought nobody would see.”
But then she said something that made my blood run cold.
“Before you open those seven boxes, you deserve to know what happened to me while you were gone.”
“Gabriel, fifteen years ago, when we got married, I was already pregnant.”
“I never told you because you were terrified of becoming a father. You had just started your first company, and you told me children would destroy your ambitions.”
I had told her I wanted to build something extraordinary before having a family.
“I respected your wishes. But I lost the baby eleven weeks into the pregnancy.”
“Nobody knows about that. Not even your mother. I went to the hospital alone because you were in London negotiating your first major investment.”
I’d been celebrating a multimillion-dollar deal.
“I buried that pain quietly,” she continued. “I thought we would have another chance.”
